Benign Cystic Tumors
Unicameral Bone Cyst
Overview
Definition and Demographics
Simple cyst; solitary
Benign fluid-filled cavity
Uni = one; camera = chamber
Not technically a neoplasm; rather, it is more likely a reactive lesion
Epidemiology
3% of all bone tumors
2:1 male predominance
Most frequently occur in the first two decades of life; mean age at presentation is 9 years1
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Proximal humerus is the most common site of occurrence
Frequently occurs in the proximal femur, which, with the proximal humerus, account for most
affected sites
Also can occur in the calcaneus and the axial skeleton, although far less often
Etiology and Genetics
The true etiology remains unclear.

Etiology and Genetics
No data support any genetic mutations that contribute to this process; therefore, this is
not a true neoplasm. The leading theory is that a region of increased pressure exists
within the medullary canal, potentially caused by venous obstructions, that may lead to
local necrosis and, in turn, to accumulation of interstitial fluid within the remaining

to contain interleukins, prostaglandins, and metalloproteinases3 (Resource 1).
Natural History
Controversial

Natural History
It was previously thought that these had the potential to resolve without intervention
after skeletal maturity is achieved. Although this can occur, it is unclear from the
literature whether this happens with any consistency (Figure 1). Radiographically, the
cysts have been shown to have low rates of complete healing, regardless whether
surgical management is performed. However, radiographic resolution does not seem to
be required for a good functional outcome. A pathologic fracture was previously thought
to stimulate cyst healing; although this can occur, it occurs in less than 10% of patients.4

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Unicameral bone cysts (UBCs) can be diagnosed via plain radiography alone. Patient history
and clinical examination may not have considerable utility in the absence of an acute injury or
pathologic fracture. These lesions may be found incidentally. Advanced imaging studies are
not required but may be useful for confirming diagnosis if the lesions present in unusual
locations or have an abnormal appearance.
Patient History
Pain

Patient History
Pain may be present because of increased stress in the region of the lesion as a result of
cortical thinning, and this may be an indicator of impending pathologic fracture. Pain

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001060
4/81

also may occur if a pathologic fracture is present. The patient may note the onset of pain
after relatively minor trauma. Associated swelling or deformity also may be present.
Approximately 80% to 85% of patients present because of a pathologic fracture5,6
Physical Examination
Pain
Swelling
Deformity
Decreased range of motion (ie, at the shoulder or hip)

Physical Examination
Pertinent physical examination findings are present if the patient has experienced a
pathologic fracture. With impending pathologic fracture, physical examination findings
may be limited.
Imaging Studies
Plain Radiography
Imaging modality of choice for initial evaluation; often may be diagnostic (Figure 2)
Lytic
Metaphyseal
Central positioning within the medullary canal, dissimilar from an aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC),
which sits eccentrically within the medullary canal
Well-circumscribed; narrow zone of transition
May be mildly expansile; does not expand the cortex as aggressively as an ABC and does not
expand the cortex wider than the adjacent physis
One chamber: there may be internal septations complicating the interpretation of the
radiograph, particularly if pathologic fracture(s) have occurred
Cortical thinning, but no cortical breakthrough in the absence of pathologic fracture
No soft-tissue mass

Active cyst: within 1 cm of or adjacent to the physis
Latent cyst: more than 1 cm from the physis
With skeletal growth, the UBC may migrate away from the physis and toward the diaphysis
Radiographic parameters for cyst healing
Complete healing is defined as more than 95% opacification of the cyst with cortical
thickening 
Partial healing is defined as more than 80% to 95% opacification of the cyst with or without
cortical thickening
Incomplete healing is defined as less than 80% opacification of the cyst with no cortical
thickening1
Modified Neer classification
I, Healed: cyst filled with new bone with or without small radiolucent area(s) less than 1 cm
in size
II, Healed with defects: radiolucent areas less than 50% of the diameter of the bone with
enough cortical thickness to prevent fracture
III, Persistent cyst: radiolucent area greater than 50% of the diameter of the bone and with
a thin cortical rim; no increase in size of the cyst
IV, Recurrent cyst: cyst reappeared in previously obliterated area or a radiolucent area has
increased in size7
Pathologic fracture: the fallen leaf sign

Plain Radiography
The fallen leaf sign is a small fracture fragment from the cortex that falls into the cyst
chamber and appears to be floating within the chamber, similar to a leaf floating
through the air. This finding is considered pathognomonic because it indicates only fluid

with this finding.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Not required for evaluation
Homogenous low signal on T1-weighted images
Homogenous signal on T2-weighted images
T1-weighted images can be used to evaluate for fracture risk
Fluid levels may be present if MRI is being performed at or near the time of a pathologic
fracture because blood will be present within the lesion as a result of fracture hematoma

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI can be used to evaluate lesions in locations that are unusual or that are less clearly
imaged via radiography. They also can be used for diagnostic confirmation and, if
management is indicated, for preoperative planning. MRI may be difficult to interpret if
obtained at the time of a pathologic fracture or during the acute healing process
because of the presence of edema, fracture hematoma, and fracture healing.
Computed Tomography
Not required for evaluation

Computed Tomography
To limit radiation exposure, CT should be avoided in children unless absolutely
necessary. CT scans may provide more detail for pathologic fractures and better
delineate cortical thinning and fracture risk than plain radiography. Overall, CT is of

integrity of the cortex and does not risk radiation exposure.
Differential Diagnosis
ABC
Enchondroma
Fibrous dysplasia
Intraosseous ganglion
Pathology
Gross
Single fluid-filled cavity; multilocular lesions can occur
Fluid
Straw-colored
Proteinaceous
Not bloody unless a pathologic fracture has occurred
Histologic
Fibrous cyst wall/lining is usually all that is available for microscopic evaluation
No epithelium or endothelium
No lakes of red blood cells, as with ABC; however, red blood cells may be present within the
lining if the tissue is sent in the setting of pathologic fracture
May contain scattered giant cells
Evidence of inflammation
Granulation tissue
Any bone is nonreactive and generally normal in appearance.
If cyst fluid is aspirated and sent for histochemical evaluation, it will contain prostaglandins,
metalloproteinases, and interleukins.3

Management

Overview
Overall, management of UBCs remains controversial. Literature supports nonsurgical
and surgical approaches and many and varied surgical techniques. To date, no
randomized prospective studies have evaluated the effectiveness of nonsurgical
management as a control protocol. An ongoing randomized controlled trial, Simple Bone
Cysts in Kids, compares two surgical treatment options without a nonsurgical control
(Resource 2). No consensus exists on the role of nonsurgical management or the
preferred surgical treatment option.8
Biopsy
UBCs do not require biopsy for diagnosis.

Biopsy
Plain radiographs are characteristic, and advanced imaging studies may be obtained to
confirm the diagnosis. If the lesion is being managed surgically, a biopsy should be
obtained at the time of the definitive procedure.vFrozen section interpretation may be
difficult because the cyst wall/lining is the only portion of the lesion that is potentially
pathologically diagnostic, and cyst wall/lining material is not always abundant at the time
of surgery. If imaging studies raise concerns about malignancy rather than a UBC, a
frozen section should be sent for analysis, and the definitive procedure should be
staged.
Nonsurgical Management
Observation may be indicated for lesions with the following characteristics:
Are found incidentally
Are asymptomatic

Appear to have a low associated risk for fracture
Nonsurgical management typically is not recommended for lesions in the proximal femur.
This is because of the increased risk of fracture secondary to the joint reactive forces across
the hip on a regular basis, potentially leading to growth arrest, the detrimental effects of
varus malunion, and the risk of osteonecrosis. Therefore, proximal femur lesions are
managed via a more aggressive surgical approach.
Medical therapy: no recommended medical therapy available
Surgical Management
May be indicated for lesions with the following characteristics
Are painful
Are progressing during the observation period
Have a high associated risk of pathologic fracture (this risk is associated with a transverse
cyst diameter that is >85% of the diameter of the affected bone and a cyst wall/lining <0.5
mm thick)9-11
Have fractured multiple times
Are located in the proximal femur
The clinician must consider the age of the patient and the proximity of the cyst to the physis in
selecting surgical management.
Growth arrest or angular deformity may result if the physis is not protected during the
procedure.
A higher risk of recurrence may exist if the cyst is incompletely managed surgically secondary
to concern about the physis.
Techniques
Aspiration and injection
Methylprednisolone
15% to 88% recurrence rate
Autologous bone marrow aspirate
52% healing rate
13% recurrence rate
Autologous bone marrow aspirate combined with demineralized bone matrix
58% healing rate

Calcium sulfate bone graft substitute
Apatitic calcium phosphate bone graft substitute
Failure of injection is defined as no evidence of radiographic healing over a 3-month period;
after three failed injections, proceeding with more aggressive surgical management may be
necessary.
Curettage and bone grafting with or without internal fixation

Surgical Management
With curettage and grafting, overall healing rates are 25% to 30%. Allograft is preferred.
The use of calcium sulfate pellets as bone graft substitute has shown more promising
results with a 66% healing rate and a 25% recurrence rate. Internal fixation is indicated
in proximal femur cysts, whereas it generally is not necessary in proximal humerus cysts.
Decompression

Decompression
Decompression refers to technical disruption of the cyst wall/lining with instruments
including, but not limited to: needles, currettes, titanium, elastic nails, Kirschner wires,
and cannulated screws. Healing rates with decompression alone involving the use of
titanium elastic nails have been reported to be as high as 73%, with recurrence rates as
low as less than 10%. Decompression can be combined with injection of a preferred
adjuvant. A potential disadvantage to using titanium elastic nails for decompression is
removal is required later.1,12
Outcomes

Outcomes

Outcomes are variable depending on cyst size, cyst location, and management strategies
used. If surgical management is attempted, recurrence is common and continued
management usually is required. Nonsurgical management may lead to recurrent
fractures, deformity, growth arrest, pain, and functional limitations. The most important
consideration for UBCs at this point, pending additional research, is that radiographic
healing of the cyst is not necessarily linked to a good clinical and functional
outcome.13,14
Aneurysmal Bone Cysts
Overview
Definition and Demographics
Benign, cystic bone lesion with multiple blood-filled cavities15 (Resource 3)
Most affected patients are aged 5 to 20 years
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Location: Found in the metaphysis of long bones but can occur in the pelvic bones, spine, and
tarsal bones
Genetics
Most primary ABCs have a ubiquitin-specific protease 6 (USP6) fusion gene (most commonly
with CDH11); however, these are not found in secondary ABCs.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Because it is a benign aggressive lesion, as per the Enneking classification, patients may
demonstrate pain, swelling, and a pathologic fracture. Spine involvement may result in spinal
cord compression and associated symptoms.
Imaging Studies
Radiography

On radiographs, ABCs appear as metaphyseal lucent lesions with cortical expansion and
thinning, as well as formation of a neocortex.
Septations may be apparent within the lesion. Although they may begin as eccentric lesions,
they can quickly expand to involve the entire metaphysis and then cause ballooning.
Dissimilar from UBCs, ABCs can expand beyond the width of the adjacent physis.
Computed Tomography
CT can more clearly demonstrate neocortex formation.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI demonstrates cortical expansion and multiple fluid levels separated by fibrous septations,
which are typical but not pathognomonic of ABCs (Figure 3).
Secondary ABCs can take over the initial lesion’s space, which may no longer demonstrate the
characteristics of the primary tumor. The only indication may be the location (eg, in the
epiphysis versus the metaphysis).

Differential Diagnosis
ABCs and telangiectatic osteosarcoma share clinical and radiographic features; however, the
tumor cells within the septae of telangiectatic osteosarcoma show cytologic atypia.
ABCs may have abundant giant cells; however, a giant cell tumor can be distinguished from an
ABC by its epiphyseal location in skeletally mature bone and the presence of sheets of giant
cells without the other features observed in an ABC.
Pathology
Histologic
Blood-filled spaces with thin, fibrous septae, no endothelial lining, and chronic inflammatory
cells with osteoclast-like giant cells (Figure 4)
Lesion periphery includes a fibrous layer with reactive bone trabeculae.
Cellular atypia and atypical mitoses are not observed.

Management
Extended intralesional curettage with high-speed burring (Resource 4)
Adjuvants, such as argon beam, phenol/alcohol, liquid nitrogen, and polymethyl methacrylate,
have been advocated. None shows superiority in decreasing recurrence risk.
En bloc resection in expendable bones
Outcomes
Rate of local recurrence is less than 20%
Recurrence usually is associated with insufficient curettage, younger patients who have open
physes, and periarticular lesions16 (Resource 5).
Cartilaginous Tumors
Enchondroma
Overview
Definition and Demographics
Benign intramedullary tumor of hyaline cartilage17 (Resource 6)
Commonly occurs in patients in their twenties to thirties but affects a wide age range
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Location
Small tubular bones of hands or feet (most common), distal femur, and proximal humerus
Rarely observed in the axial skeleton
Most common bone tumor of the hand
Pathophysiology
Thought to be the result of abnormal endochondral ossification from chondroblasts trapped
within the intramedullary space at the level of the metaphysis, which begin to proliferate

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Incidentally discovered
Usually painless, unless a pathologic fracture of phalanges of the hands or feet is present
May present as multiple enchondromatosis in patients with Maffucci or Ollier syndromes
Maffucci syndrome manifests as subcutaneous hemangiomas of the hands and feet
Patients with Ollier syndrome have dysplastic bones with enchondromas in the metaphysis
and diaphysis, typically unilateral, resulting in shortening, deformity, and increased risk of
fracture (Figure 5). Visceral tumors also can develop in the ovaries and liver. Enchondromas
in these patients typically do not grow past skeletal maturity; however, clinical and
radiographic follow-up is necessary because of the increased risk of malignant
transformation18 (Resource 7).

On radiographs enchondromas are metaphyseal and typically central, with a narrow zone of
transition and a variable internal matrix of mineralization.
In the short tubular bones of the hands and feet, enchondromas are more lucent, with
minimal mineralization.
Radiographs are sufficient to make a diagnosis; however, cross-sectional imaging studies
should be obtained in older patients with pain, increased lucencies, endosteal scalloping,
cortical response with thickening, or cortical breakthrough because these signs may be
indicative of a more aggressive lesion19 (Resource 8).
Computed Tomography
Useful in evaluating for endosteal scalloping
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Useful in evaluating for bone marrow edema (suggestive of impending pathologic fracture)
and soft-tissue extension
Pathology
Histologic
On low-power images, cartilage surrounded by cancellous bone
On higher power images, hypocellular areas of chondroblasts surrounded by hyaline cartilage
In the hands and feet, may have increased cellularity and some nuclear atypia; therefore, a
multidisciplinary approach with clinical, radiographic, and histologic correlation is paramount.
Management
Asymptomatic tumors are managed via observation.
Symptomatic lesions are managed via curettage and grafting, with or without fixation.
In patients with a fracture, thorough curettage must be performed before grafting/fixation.
Historically, pathologic fractures through the phalanges of the hand were initially immobilized,
with curettage performed after healing. This may result in prolonged immobilization;
therefore, single-stage curettage and fixation is advocated20 (Resource 9)
In patients with open physes and a stable fracture, surgical treatment can be delayed until
after healing and the lesion is away from the physis to avoid the risk of growth arrest.

Recurrence rate is low; therefore, curettage generally is curative.
Solitary Osteochondroma
Overview
Definition and Demographics
Benign chondrogenic tumor resulting in a prominent bony and cartilaginous outgrowth
Occurs in the first and second decade of life and commonly manifests in the adolescent
population
No noted male or female predominance
Epidemiology
Most common benign lesion of bone

Epidemiology
They account for 30% of all benign bone tumors and approximately 10% of all bone
tumors. The incidence likely is underestimated because of a potentially large number of
patients with asymptomatic lesions who do not present for evaluation21 (Resource 10).
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Most frequently located about the knee
Distal femur
Proximal tibia
Proximal fibula
Also occur in the following locations
Proximal humerus
Proximal femur
Axial skeleton
Subungual

Solitary osteochondromas are located in the metaphyseal region of the bone and are adjacent
to the physis.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Lesions are oriented away from the adjacent articular surface and physis, and they also
grow in that direction. Osteochondromas that occur in the epiphysis and are oriented
toward the articular surface result from a different pathologic process called dysplasia
epiphysealis hemimelica (Trevor disease). Pedunculated osteochondromas are
connected to the medullary canal with a narrow stalk/stem. Sessile osteochondromas
are connected to the medullary canal via a broad base rather than a stalk and generally
flatter in nature. The stalk or base osteochondroma consists of cortical and cancellous
bone that is contiguous with the medullary canal, and the mass itself consists of a
cartilaginous cap that encases cancellous bone.
Etiology and Genetics
True neoplasms that are the result of a genetic mutation

Etiology and Genetics
Previously, it was thought that osteochondromas were the result of an abnormality
related to physeal growth; however, they currently are known to be the result of a
mutation that results in the loss of tumor suppressor function of the EXT gene. The
mutation in the EXT-1 gene is known to occur in patients with solitary osteochondroma
(specifically inactivation of both copies of EXT-1 in the cartilaginous cap). Multiple
mutations in EXT-1 and EXT-2 are responsible for hereditary multiple exostosis.21,22 The
neoplastic process is thought to occur in the cartilaginous cap portion of the tumor
rather than in the perichondrial ring or the bony portion of the lesion.
Natural History

Growth of the lesion and migration away from the physis is expected until skeletal maturity is
reached.
Malignant degeneration

Natural History
Lesions that continue to grow or demonstrate new growth after skeletal maturity is
reached should be evaluated for malignant degeneration. Lesions that become newly
painful after skeletal maturity without an ostensible mechanical explanation for that pain
should be evaluated for malignant degeneration.
Less than 1% of solitary osteochondromas are said to undergo malignant degeneration
to low-grade chondrosarcoma. This statistic is outdated (from textbooks and papers
published in the 1950s, 1970s, and early 1980s) and often cited but likely overestimates
the true risk of malignant degeneration. The true incidence of solitary osteochondroma
is unknown. Given the assumption that many more of these lesions are present in the
population but are not being evaluated, the denominator for this statistic likely is much
larger. It also likely suffers from selection bias because sarcomas generally are rare and
published cases involve patients who sought treatment at the reporting tertiary and
quaternary referral centers.23
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Overview

Overview
Similar to many benign bone tumors, osteochondromas may manifest as an incidental
finding. However, they also may manifest as painful and, sometimes, growing masses
that alarm parents and primary care providers. Both clinical and radiographic
evaluations provide useful information in the work up of these patients. Advanced

appearance.
Patient History
Patients may have an incidentally found painless mass.
An increase in size of a previously identified lesion may prompt the evaluation.
Pain may be a presenting symptom.

Patient History
Typically, pain is the result of compression of surrounding neurovascular structures (if
the lesion is in the posteromedial distal femur or the proximal fibula); bursal
inflammation; muscular impingement or irritation; or, uncommonly, fracture of the stalk
of a pedunculated osteochondroma.21
Physical Examination
Palpable, fixed bony mass in the metaphyseal region; may demonstrate slight movement if the
osteochondroma is pedunculated with a fractured stalk
No overlying skin changes
No associated soft-tissue masses
Neurovascular examination may reveal abnormalities if the osteochondroma is compressing
or impinging on surrounding structures
Numbness
Weakness
Decreased pulses or slow capillary refill
Palpable snapping may be present over the osteochondroma with motion of the adjacent
joint, particularly if the osteochondroma is pedunculated and in the distal lateral femur
(iliotibial band) or the proximal medial tibia (hamstring insertion).

Plain Radiography
Preferred imaging modality for initial evaluation (Figure 6)
Often the only imaging modality required for diagnostic purposes
Findings
A solitary osteochondroma will appear as a protuberant metaphyseal lesion on plain
radiographs. Osteochondromas typically are adjacent to the physis but oriented away from
the physis and the articular surface. They may be pedunculated or sessile. Osteochondromas
must demonstrate corticomedullary continuity; if this feature is lacking, surgeons should
suspect a more aggressive lesion, such as juxtacortical or surface osteosarcoma.
Intralesional calcifications that appear as rings and arcs peripherally within the cartilaginous
cap
Intralesional calcifications should be minimal in a true osteochondroma. More substantial
intralesional calcification raise concern regarding a more aggressive lesion, such as
chondrosarcoma. The cartilaginous cap itself appears radiolucent on plain radiographs. No
associated periosteal reaction, soft-tissue mass, or other aggressive features should be
observed.
